summary: This informational memo describes how to invoke transcoding services in SIP using third-party call control. This meets the requirements for supporting deaf, hard of hearing and speech-impaired users.

plainLanguage.summary: If two people use different media formats, a helper in the middle can translate. This document explains how to bring that helper into the call, which helps people who cannot hear or speak.

questions: sip transcoding third party call control
how to invoke transcoding in sip
how to convert audio to text in sip
subtitle: How to bring a transcoding server into a SIP call to convert between different media formats.

tldr.problem: Two SIP users may discover they cannot communicate because they support different media codecs or formats (for example, one expects audio, another needs text). There is no standard way to insert a transcoding service into the conversation.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC describes how to use third-party call control (3pcc) to establish two separate SIP sessions: one between the first user and a transcoding server, and another between the transcoding server and the second user. The transcoder translates between the two streams.
tldr.outcome: Deaf, hard of hearing, and speech-impaired users can now participate in calls with hearing users or text-only systems by invoking transcoding services that convert speech to text and text back to speech.

facts.label: Media streams per session pair
facts.value: Two bidirectional streams (four total: A-T, T-A, B-T, T-B)

facts.label: Common use case
facts.value: Speech-to-text and text-to-speech conversion for accessibility

facts.label: Session prerequisite
facts.value: Transcoder must confirm with 200 OK before callee is alerted

today: RFC 4117 is an informational specification describing one method for transcoding invocation. While SIP has evolved with many extensions since 2005, the 3pcc approach described here remains valid and is used in modern accessibility solutions for video relay services and captioning.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
SIP (Session Initiation Protocol) is used to set up multimedia calls. The problem this RFC addresses is codec incompatibility: when user A wants to send audio but user B only accepts text, or when different audio codecs are involved, the call cannot proceed without help.

The RFC describes how to use third-party call control (3pcc), a SIP technique where an intermediary device manages sessions on behalf of multiple participants. A transcoding server acts as this intermediary, establishing a session with user A to receive one format, transforming the content, and establishing another session with user B to send the other format.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of SIP as a system for setting up phone calls. When two people can't understand each other's format, you need someone to translate. 3pcc lets the phone system automatically arrange that.

sections.title: General Model and Flow
sections.content:
The basic model involves three parties: user A (the caller), user B (the callee), and T (the transcoding server). Depending on who initiates transcoding, the flows differ.

The RFC shows two main scenarios: callee-invoked transcoding (B decides it needs transcoding and contacts T) and caller-invoked transcoding (A decides transcoding is needed). In callee invocation, B receives an INVITE from A, recognizes a format problem, and invokes T while responding to A. The transcoder establishes media paths to both users and translates between them.
sections.plainLanguage: Three parties: the person calling, the person receiving, and the translator in the middle. Either one can ask for the translator, and the translator connects to both.

sections.title: Session Establishment and Media Streams
sections.content:
When the callee invokes transcoding, B sends an INVITE to T including both A's session description and B's desired format in a single SDP. T responds with a 200 OK containing the addresses where it wants to receive media from both A and B. This establishes four media streams: audio from A to T, text from T to B, text from B to T, and audio from T back to A.

Each party exchanges session descriptions (SDP) to negotiate codecs and transport addresses. The transcoder's role is to listen on its advertised addresses, read the incoming stream (say, audio from A), transform it (convert to text), and send it out on the address where B is listening. It does the reverse for B's text stream.
sections.plainLanguage: Three phone numbers: where A talks, where T listens to A, where B listens, and where T listens to B. The transcoder sits in the middle, taking what one person sends and converting it to what the other needs.

sections.title: Invoking Transcoding and Parallel Services
sections.content:
The RFC also covers two advanced scenarios: parallel transcoding (multiple transcoders running at the same time, each providing a different service) and serial transcoding (output of one transcoder feeds into another). These allow complex transformations, such as speech-to-text followed by machine translation to a different language.

The key principle in all flows is that the transcoding service must confirm availability with a 200 OK response before the callee is alerted. This ensures the transcoder is ready to handle the session, reducing the risk that the callee accepts but the transcoder fails.
sections.plainLanguage: You can have multiple translators working in parallel (each translating to a different language) or in series (one translates speech to text, the next translates that text to a different language).

sections.title: Security and Preconditions
sections.content:
The RFC notes that preconditions (defined in other SIP RFCs) can be used to make transcoding more reliable by preventing the callee from being alerted until the transcoding session is fully established. This avoids the awkward situation where a user accepts a call but the transcoder is not ready.

The document also mentions that implementers should be aware of the network requirements: third-party call control requires the transcoding server to be able to contact all parties and to maintain multiple SIP sessions simultaneously. The actual security aspects (authentication, encryption) are addressed in other SIP RFCs.
sections.plainLanguage: Make sure the translator is really ready before telling the other person the call is coming. Otherwise, they answer but the translator is not there yet.
